chapter_12.title: European Society in the Age of the Renaissance

terms.definition: A period of cultural rebirth and artistic/intellectual flowering in Europe, originating in Italy.
Financial support of writers and artists by cities, groups, and wealthy individuals, often to produce specific works or buy prestige.
Sworn associations of free citizens seeking urban independence from local nobles.
Disenfranchised and heavily taxed common people in Italian cities who resented exclusion from power.
Governors or despots who held absolute power in Italian city-states.
Splendid households and palaces where signori and oligarchs conducted state business and displayed patronage.
A program of study emphasizing the critical study of Latin and Greek literature with the goal of understanding human nature.
The quality of being able to shape the world according to one's own will; human agency and individual capability.
Northern humanists who interpreted Italian ideas about and attitudes toward antiquity in terms of their own religious traditions.
A debate among writers and thinkers beginning in the fifteenth century about women's qualities and proper role in society.
Term applied to Jews and Muslims who accepted Christianity, frequently viewed with suspicion by Spanish authorities and the Inquisition.
Widespread opposition to the clergy, driven by clerical immorality, ignorance, and pluralism.
A document issued by the Catholic Church lessening penance or time in purgatory, viewed by critics as corrupt.
The followers of Luther and other reformers who protested the practices and doctrines of the Catholic Church.
The fleet sent by Philip II of Spain in 1588 against England as a religious crusade; its defeat marked the beginning of Spain's decline.

terms.term: The Institutes of the Christian Religion
terms.definition: John Calvin's foundational formulation of Christian theology, which laid out the core doctrines of Calvinism.
John Calvin's religious theory that God has already planned out a person's life and salvation before birth.
The official Roman Catholic agency founded in 1542 to combat international doctrinal heresy.
Members of the Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius Loyola, aimed at spreading the Catholic faith through education and missionary work.
French Calvinists.
Catholic and Protestant moderates in 16th-century France who held that only a strong monarchy could save France from collapse.
A document issued by Henry IV of France in 1598 granting liberty of conscience and public worship to Calvinists.
The alliance of seven northern provinces that declared their independence from Spain as the United Provinces of the Netherlands.
Spanish for 'conqueror'; Spanish soldier-explorers seeking to conquer the New World for the Spanish crown.
A small, maneuverable, three-masted sailing ship developed by the Portuguese in the fifteenth century.
A second-century work that synthesized classical knowledge of geography and introduced longitude and latitude.
1494 agreement brokered by the Pope dividing the Atlantic discoveries between Spain and Portugal.
Also known as the Aztec Empire, a large and complex Native civilization in modern-day Mexico conquered by Cortés.
Vast Andean empire centered in Peru conquered by Francisco Pizarro.
The administrative units used by Spain to govern its vast territories in the New World.
A system whereby the Spanish crown granted conquerors the right to forcibly employ groups of Indians; a disguised form of slavery.
The extensive movement of peoples, animals, plants, cultures, and diseases between the Old and New Worlds.
The series of treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648 and marked the end of large-scale religious violence in Europe.
A series of violent uprisings during the early reign of Louis XIV triggered by growing royal control and taxation.
A system of economic regulations aimed at increasing the power of the state based on the belief that a nation's international power is based on its wealth.
A series of treaties from 1713 that ended the War of the Spanish Succession, ended French expansion in Europe, and marked the rise of the British Empire.
The nobility of Prussia and Brandenburg, who were reluctant allies of Frederick William in the consolidation of the Prussian absolutist state.
The highest-ranking members of the Russian nobility.
Free groups and outlaw warrior bands of peasants in southern Russia who formed alliances with the Russian state while maintaining autonomy.
The ruler of the Ottoman Empire, who possessed all the agricultural land of the empire and inspected it through bureaucratic armies.
The core of the Ottoman sultan's army, composed of slave conscripts from non-Muslim parts of the empire.
A system used by the Ottomans in which subjects were divided into religious communities, with each millet enjoying autonomous self-government under its religious leaders.
A form of government in which power is limited by law and balanced between the authority and power of the government on the one hand and the rights and liberties of the subjects on the other.
A form of government in which there is no monarch and power rests in the hands of the people as exercised through elected representatives.
Members of a 16th- and 17th-century reform movement within the Church of England that advocated purifying it of Roman Catholic elements.
English military dictatorship (1653–1658) established by Oliver Cromwell following the execution of Charles I.

Legislation passed by the English Parliament in 1673 to secure the position of the Anglican Church by stripping Puritans, Catholics, and other dissenters of voting, preaching, and holding public office.
The executive officer in each of the United Provinces of the Netherlands, often a politician from the House of Orange.
An early modern term for the study of the nature of the universe, its purpose, and how it functioned; it encompassed what we would call science today.
The idea that the sun, not the earth, was the center of the universe.
The approach, pioneered by Galileo, of conducting controlled experiments rather than relying on abstract speculation.
Law formulated by Galileo that rest is not the natural state of objects, but rather that an object continues in motion forever unless stopped by some external force.

Newton's law that all bodies in the universe attract one another in a mathematically precise way, with the force of attraction proportional to the quantity of matter and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
A theory of inductive reasoning that calls for acquiring evidence through observation and experimentation rather than deductive reason and speculation.
Descartes's view that all of reality could be reduced to two entities: mind and matter.
The influential intellectual and cultural movement of the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries that introduced a new worldview based on the use of reason, the scientific method, and progress.
A secular, critical way of thinking in which nothing was to be accepted on faith, and everything was to be submitted to the rationalism of reason.
French intellectuals of the Enlightenment who championed reason, criticized traditional religion, and advocated social reform.
The transition in Europe from a society where literacy consisted of patriarchal and communal reading of religious texts to a society where reading was individual, silent, and consumed diverse texts.
Regular social gatherings held by talented and rich Parisian women in their homes, where philosophers and commoners met to discuss literature, science, and philosophy.
A popular style in Europe in the eighteenth century, known for its soft pastels, ornate interiors, sentimental portraits, and starry-eyed lovers.
An idealized intellectual social space that emerged during the Enlightenment, where the public came together to discuss important societal issues.
Term coined by historians to describe the rule of eighteenth-century monarchs who adopted Enlightenment reforms without surrendering their absolute political power.
View that monarchy was the best form of government, that all elements of society should serve the monarch, and that the state should use its resources and authority to improve society.
The Jewish Enlightenment of the second half of the eighteenth century, led by Moses Mendelssohn.
The movement to fence in common lands in order to create large, consolidated farms, held by owners and worked by landless laborers.
The transformation of large numbers of small peasant farmers into landless wage-earning rural laborers.
A business or manufacturing activity carried on in a person's home, heavily featuring the putting-out system for textiles.
A merchant-capitalist system in which merchants loaned raw materials to rural workers, who processed them and returned the finished products to the merchant.
The shift that occurred as families in northwestern Europe focused on wage earning rather than producing goods for household consumption, reducing leisure time and increasing consumer demand.
The organization of artisanal production into trade-based associations, each of which received a monopoly over its trade and the right to train apprentices and hire workers.
The belief in free trade and competition based on Adam Smith's argument that the invisible hand of free competition benefits all individuals.
English laws passed in the seventeenth century requiring that goods imported into England and its colonies be carried on British ships, severely hurting Dutch trade supremacy.
The 1763 treaty that ended the Seven Years' War, ceding French territory in North America and India to Great Britain.
A form of serfdom in which a planter or rancher kept workers in perpetual debt bondage by advancing food, money, and shelter.
The forced migration of millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries.

chapter_18.title: Life in the Era of Expansion

terms.definition: A cooperative economic and moral safety net practiced by rural communities to maintain public order and police personal behavior.
Coercive, degrading public-shaming rituals used by village communities to police personal behavior and marital deviance.
The sharp increase in out-of-wedlock births that occurred in Europe between 1750 and 1850.
The business practice of hiring peasant women to breastfeed noble and upper-class infants.
Events such as bullbaiting and cockfighting that involved inflicting violence and death on animals and that were popular with the European masses.
The raucous, temporary festival preceding Lent that allowed ordinary people to invert social hierarchies and engage in feasting.
The idea that prices should be fair, protecting consumers against price gouging, which frequently sparked popular bread riots.
The wide-ranging growth in consumption and new attitudes toward consumer goods that emerged in northwestern Europe.
A Protestant revival movement in the early eighteenth century that emphasized a warm, emotional religion and Christian rebirth.
Protestant group founded by John Wesley emphasizing emotional religious commitment and methodical devotion among the working classes.
A sect of Catholicism originating with Cornelius Jansen that emphasized heavy asceticism and predestination, outlawed by papal and royal authorities.

chapter_19.title: Revolutions in Politics (French Revolution and Napoleon)

terms.definition: A legislative body in pre-revolutionary France made up of representatives of each of the three classes: clergy, nobility, and commoners.
The three legal orders of France: the clergy (First Estate), the nobility (Second Estate), and everyone else (Third Estate).
The first French revolutionary legislature, made up primarily of representatives of the Third Estate.
The panic that swept rural France in the summer of 1789 as peasants feared nobles were hiring brigands to destroy crops.
A political club in revolutionary France whose members were well-educated radical republicans.
From 1792 to 1793, the second phase of the French Revolution, during which the fall of the French monarchy introduced a rapid radicalization.
A moderate faction of the Jacobin club that favored spreading the revolution internationally.
Radical Jacobin faction led by Robespierre and Danton that sat on the highest benches in the National Convention.
The laboring poor and radical artisans of Paris who wore trousers and pushed the revolution into its radical phase.
The period from 1793 to 1794 during which Robespierre's Committee of Public Safety tried and executed thousands suspected of treason.
A reaction to the violence of the Reign of Terror in 1794 resulting in Robespierre's execution and a loosening of economic controls.
French civil code of 1804 reasserting legal equality of male citizens and absolute security of private property.
The empire over which Napoleon and his allies ruled, encompassing virtually all of Europe except Great Britain and Russia.
Napoleon's economic blockade designed to isolate Great Britain and destroy its trade.
The burst of major inventions and economic expansion that began in Britain in the late eighteenth century.
A simple, inexpensive, hand-powered spinning machine created by James Hargreaves.
A spinning machine created by Richard Arkwright that used waterpower and required a larger mill.
A breakthrough invention powered by coal that transformed energy use and fueled factory output.
George Stephenson's famous early steam locomotive that achieved unprecedented speeds.
An architectural landmark made of glass and iron in London that hosted the Great Exhibition of 1851.
David Ricardo's theory suggesting that population growth prevents wages from rising above subsistence levels.
Government taxation on imported foreign goods designed to shield domestic industries.
Pioneering British laws passed in the 1830s and 1840s that limited child labor hours and set safety standards.
Gender-role ideology placing men in public wage-earning work and women in domestic housekeeping.
British law prohibiting underground work in mines for all women and girls as well as boys under ten.
Awareness of belonging to a distinct social and economic class whose interests conflict with other classes.
Handicraft workers who attacked factories in northern England, smashing new machines they blamed for job losses.
British laws passed in 1799 outlawing unions and strikes.
A meeting of the Quadruple Alliance (Russia, Prussia, Austria, Great Britain) and France held to fashion a general peace settlement after the defeat of Napoleon.
Treaty formed by Russia, Prussia, and Austria in 1815 to suppress liberal and revolutionary movements across Europe.
Repressive laws enacted in the German Confederation in 1819 to censor liberal ideas and suppress student organizations.
A philosophy whose principal ideas were equality and liberty; liberals demanded representative government and equality before the law.
A doctrine of economic liberalism that calls for unrestricted private enterprise and no government interference in the economy.
The idea that each people has its own specific unity and common history serving as the basis for an independent state.
A radical political and economic ideology calling for economic planning, cooperation, and an end to private property.
Political and economic philosophy based on the writings of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, emphasizing class struggle and the ultimate overthrow of capitalism.
The middle class, who owned the means of production and employed the proletariat according to Marxist theory.
The industrial working class who, according to Marx, were exploited by the bourgeoisie.
A movement in art, literature, and music characterized by emotional exuberance, unrestrained imagination, and an intense focus on nature.
High British tariffs on imported grain that benefited wealthy landowners while hurting the poor; repealed in 1846.
A peaceful protest in Manchester in 1819 that was violently broken up by armed cavalry.
British law that expanded the electorate, eliminated rotten boroughs, and shifted political power toward the industrial urban middle class.
The four years of potato crop failure in Ireland (1845–1848) that led to mass starvation and emigration.
A liberal plan for German national unification that included the German-speaking parts of the Austrian Empire.
